status_reason: Material (whole milk), targets (fat and protein), location (pipe) and lab reference values are known; the transmission concept is blocked for opaque milk, but a reflection-based NIR test is supported by the sources.
answer: An in-line transmission probe will not work on opaque whole milk. Test a flush-mounted fiber NIR diffuse reflection probe in the milk pipe, with MSC or SNV scatter correction and PLS calibration against independent lab fat and protein values. Combining NIR with Raman is a hypothesis worth testing only if it beats NIR alone on the same validation data.

inline.headline: Test NIR diffuse reflection probe flush-mounted in the milk pipe for fat and protein, with MSC/SNV and PLS
inline.probe: fiber-optic NIR diffuse reflection probe with separate source and collection fibers
inline.install: flush-mounted in the pipe so it sees the flowing whole milk
inline.test_against: MIR ATR fiber probe, only if NIR fails validation on the same samples
inline.not_final_because: Whole milk has not been measured yet; fat globule size and surface effects must be tested; the silica fiber ends at 2400 nm while NIR is quoted to 2500 nm; no accuracy values exist for this process; reference values must be independent lab analyses.

problems.text: A transmission or transflection probe in the pipe will not work on whole milk: it is meant for transparent or semi-transparent liquids and fails when the product is too thick or fat-rich.
Reflection NIR reads only the surface and is sensitive to fat globule size, so the model needs scatter correction (MSC or SNV) and calibration over the variation seen in your process.

The silica Vis-NIR fiber transmits up to 2400 nm while NIR is quoted up to 2500 nm; the fat and protein bands at 0.85-1.1 µm lie inside the fiber range, so the choice is workable but the bands used must be confirmed.

Lab values are only a valid reference if they are independent laboratory analyses, not the instrument's own calibration; with limited data the model must be checked with segmented cross-validation and randomisation tests.

methods.why: Inline NIR reflection is the dairy method for opaque products, and the fat and protein bands lie at 0.85-1.1 µm.
It fails for thick or fat-rich product, and whole milk is opaque.
It adds molecular specificity that NIR might miss, but Raman signals are weak, masked by fluorescence, and the probe is high cost.
It adds molecular specificity, but MIR is limited to very thin layers and is used through ATR attachments.

questions.q: Is the product in the pipe only whole milk, or also concentrates or cream?
questions.why: The reflection method is named for opaque or concentrated products, so the product range sets the calibration scope.

questions.q: How many independent lab reference samples exist, and which lab methods were used for fat and protein?
questions.why: Reference values must be independent of the instrument; limited data need strict validation.

questions.q: Can the lab samples be matched in time to the spectra, and over what range do fat and protein vary in the process?
questions.why: Spectra and reference must be synchronised and must cover the operating range to build a robust model.

questions.q: Is a flush probe position possible at the pipe, and how long is the fiber run to the spectrometer?
questions.why: Probe installation and fiber length decide the practical setup.

questions.q: Is a second method (Raman or MIR ATR) acceptable in cost, if NIR alone is not accurate enough?
questions.why: Raman and MIR ATR are rated high cost, so the extra method must be justified by the results.

experiment.objective: Test whether NIR diffuse reflection on flowing whole milk predicts fat and protein against independent lab values.
steps: Install a silica Vis-NIR reflection probe flush in a pipe section or bypass with the milk flowing.
Collect spectra over the range of fat and protein in the process, with lab reference analyses taken at the same time.
Apply MSC or SNV correction, then build a PLS model for fat and protein.
Validate the model with segmented cross-validation and randomisation tests on held-out data.
Repeat the test with Raman measured on the same flow, and compare with NIR alone on the same validation data.
references: S01 p.17: inline NIR reflection for dairy
S02 p.11: silica diffuse-reflection probes tested with NIR spectrometers
S03 p.14: validation requirements when data are limited
experiment.go_no_go: Criteria come from the client; no accuracy values are given in the sources.

pathway.key_features: NIR fat and protein bands at 0.85-1.1 µm, selected by multivariate analysis.
pathway.path_reason: The target is a composition model from NIR spectra, which matches the AI-driven chemometric model path after the lab test.

multispectral.why: Dairy sources note that Raman adds molecular specificity NIR might miss, and a pharma study found NIR and Raman complementary (NIR sees polar groups, Raman the backbone).
multispectral.test: Measure NIR and Raman on the same flowing milk with the same reference values; the combination must beat NIR alone on the same validation data. Check whether the Raman signal is usable given weak signals and fluorescence.

assumptions: The product is whole milk, opaque and flowing in a pipe.
Fat and protein are the only targets.
Independent lab reference values are available for calibration.
A flush probe position is possible in the pipe.
The fiber length to the spectrometer is not yet known.
